newsitem.title: UK: Blair and Clinton launch G7 jobs initiative.
newsitem.headline: Blair and Clinton launch G7 jobs initiative.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton and British Prime Minister Tony Blair announced on Thursday they planned a joint initiative to tackle unemployment, under the umbrella of the Group of Seven industrialised countries.

They told a news conference they would ask other G7 members at next month's summit in Denver to launch a two-year plan to reduce joblessness in the main industrial countries by increasing labour market flexibility.

"In Europe, in particular, we need to reduce long-term and youth unemployment, both of which are unacceptably high," Blair said, while Clinton said he was pleased with the plan to pursue an economic agenda through the Group of Eight -- the G7 industrialised nations plus Russia.
Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer, Gordon Brown, said he would host a summit of finance and social affairs ministers from the G7 nations and Russia in London next January.
The G7's main summit will take place in the British city of Birmingham in the summer.

The ministers will swap ideas on how to give people the skills they need in the flexible labour markets of the future, ensuring tax and benefit systems promote work and removing barriers to job creation, Britain's Treasury said.
"Employability is the key to a cohesive society which offers opportunity to all its citizens," Brown said in a statement.

"Better education and higher skills, combined with reduced burdens on business, are the way to guarantee the high and stable levels of growth and employment which are the core goals of our economic policy," he added.

Officials said Clinton and Blair wanted to take advantage of the fact that the United States and Britain, whose records on jobs are probably the best in the G7, are chairing the powerful forum this year and next. Britain will take over chairmanship of the G7 in 1998.
A Blair spokesman said the two leaders felt they had transcended the barriers of left and right, taking a pragmatic approach to the problems of joblessness and welfare.

They believed the other members of the Group of Seven -- Japan, France, Germany, Italy and Canada -- could learn from their success in creating jobs by keeping labour costs low and cutting through red tape to encourage small firms.
Brown said employability -- ensuring people have the skills to get and keep jobs -- will be the focus of next year's conference.
"This is the new economic agenda. It enables us to benefit from flexible labour markets, while ensuring that everyone can share in the rewards of a more dynamic economy," he said.
"We intend to make this a key theme of both our Presidency of the G8 and of the European Union." Britain takes over the EU presidency for the first half of 1998.
G7 employment ministers have held two job summits in recent years, one in Detroit, Cleveland, and the other in Lille, northern France.
